8.0.s.en: (3) The work of God in the second return

8.0.0.en: Ahava: one of the tributaries of the Euphrates near Babylon, where there was a gathering of the Jews, since they preferred to live beside rivers so that it would be easy for them to wash when offering their worship to God, as the Psalm says, "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down" (Ps 137:1), and Ezekiel also lived in captivity beside the Chebar (Ezek 1:1). Casiphia: a word meaning silver, and it is a region in Media with silver mines, around which the Levites gathered; perhaps they worked in these mines.

8.0.1.en: 1- Ezra gathered those who wished to return from captivity at the river Ahava, and perhaps he organized them and learned their genealogies, mentioned in (vv. 1-14), and that was during three days. He discovered the presence of a number of priests and people but found none of the Levites.

8.0.2.en: 2- The gathering of the people for three days at the river is a type of the Resurrection of Christ, whose power we receive through the sacrament of Baptism and the work of the Holy Spirit in it, which the water signifies.

8.0.3.en: 3- Ezra was not content to grieve over the Levites' lack of response, but chose ten of his assistants and sent them under the leadership of two men whom he called men of understanding. All ten were heads of fathers, but two of them were distinguished by understanding and the ability to speak and persuade (v. 16). He sent these to a man named Iddo who lived in the region of Casiphia, which, as we mentioned, probably had living in it a number of Levites and Nethinim, that is, the Gentiles who helped in the service of the temple. Iddo is styled the chief, and perhaps he was the head of a school of the Levites.

8.0.4.en: 4- Ezra's assistants were able to persuade Iddo to call among the Levites and the Nethinim to return to Jerusalem, and Iddo responded, so forty of the Levites were persuaded and went to the river Ahava where Ezra was staying. As for the Nethinim, a large number of them responded, 220, and they too went to Ezra. This shows the extent of the Gentiles' response and the slackness of the Levites who were consecrated to the service of the house of God, for they loved the world and clung to their possessions, so most of them refused to return to Jerusalem. Unfortunately the Levites had already been slack about returning in the days of Zerubbabel, for only 74 Levites returned, and the reasons for that were mentioned previously in (ch. 2:40).

8.0.5.en: 5- We see Ezra's faith and humility in ascribing every blessing in the return to Jerusalem to the hand of God, for he says "according to the good hand of my God upon me" (v. 18).

8.1.0.en: After the people gathered around Ezra at the river Ahava, he proclaimed among them a communal fast, that they might cut off from themselves their material attachments to the land of captivity, for fasting is detachment and leaving the world in order to enjoy God, and by this they can overcome the wars of the devil, as Christ said, "this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting" (Mt 17:21). And if they gathered at the river Ahava, which signifies Baptism, they need, after receiving the new nature, to keep it by means of fasting, which attaches their hearts to the love of God and not the world. This is the greatest preparation for the spiritual journey, that is, returning to God, for returning to God requires weaning from the world. The journey of returning to God also requires repentance, so Ezra proclaimed humbling themselves before God, that He might accept their repentance, so that they would be cleansed from every sin and God would enlighten their eyes and they would walk in the right way and keep His commandments.

8.2.0.en: His power: His authority and strength in the war with Satan.

8.2.1.en: Ezra looked at the length of the return journey, which was about 900 miles, and at the possibility of robbers and enemies, especially since he had with him thousands of women and children, in addition to precious possessions, namely silver, gold and valuable vessels estimated at millions of pounds. In the face of these fears Ezra felt the need for protection and care.

8.2.2.en: Ezra thought of asking the king for guards to accompany him on the road, but he quickly drew back and was ashamed to ask for that, for how could he believe in a mighty God able to preserve him and ask for human help? So he rejected this thought and believed in God and relied on Him.

8.2.3.en: If Nehemiah accepted guards to accompany him from the same King Artaxerxes and thanked him for it, this does not mean that Nehemiah's faith was weak, for he too was ashamed to refuse the king's soldiers. Both Ezra and Nehemiah believed in the power of God accompanying them and preserving those with them... God works by all means, and what remains is for us to believe in His work in all circumstances.

8.3.0.en: Ezra felt reassured after he had prayed and fasted with the people and God had answered him, and he began the journey, which took about four months, and arrived in peace at Jerusalem. That is, God answered and preserved His children and those who sought Him from two things:

8.3.1.en: 1- From all the dangers that they might meet on the road.

8.3.2.en: 2- He preserved them in unity, so they did not divide against one another, but walked in unity and in submission to Ezra.

8.3.3.en: Your God is able to preserve you in the midst of all dangers. He asks only for your love, your prayers, your fasting and your seeking of Him. He wants your heart and promises you complete peace, even if you walk through the valley of the shadow of death.

8.4.0.en: Ezra chose twelve men known for faithfulness and exactness from the chief of the priests; two of them are mentioned, Sherebiah and Hashabiah.

8.4.1.en: These twelve may all have been chief priests, that is, heads of priestly divisions. Or only some of them may have been chief priests and the rest priests. Sherebiah and Hashabiah may have been the heads of the Levites mentioned in (Neh 12:24), and with them ten of the priests and Levites. In sum, they were twelve of those consecrated to the service of the house of the Lord, of the priests or the Levites.

8.5.0.en: Basin: a vessel, usually small, like a cup or a glass.

8.5.1.en: Dram of gold: equal to half a shekel, and the shekel is about 12 grams.

8.5.2.en: Polished: that is, smooth and shining.

8.5.3.en: Ezra gathered all the silver and gold and the vessels made of silver, gold and fine copper, weighed them and handed them over to these twelve, that they might carry them and keep them on the way of the journey. This shows his good distribution of responsibilities and his care to protect the precious gifts belonging to God. Consequently, if anything of them were lost, no one would think that Ezra had taken anything of them, or that any one person of the twelve had taken it, because the responsibility was collective, and all were responsible for guarding these gifts.

8.5.4.en: He specified the weights of the silver and gold and the vessels made of them, and likewise those made of copper, and handed them over to these faithful men.

8.5.5.en: We notice that these gifts were many because:

8.5.7.en: 2- Artaxerxes loved God, so he and his counselors were generous in their giving.

8.5.8.en: 3- The people gave generously to God out of their love for His house.

8.6.0.en: Ezra declared to the men that they were holy and consecrated to the service of God, and likewise that these vessels were holy to God. The holy man esteems everything that is holy and keeps it until he gives it to God, as he first gave himself to God; that is, the man who has been sanctified is entrusted with holy things. And these holy things are the gifts of the king, his counselors and the people to God, and therefore they became holy and set apart for God, no one can take them, but they are given only to the house of the Lord.

8.7.0.en: Ezra asked Sherebiah and Hashabiah and those with them to keep all that they had received throughout the journey until they reached Jerusalem, and then hand over all they had to the priests and Levites in charge of the treasuries of the house of the Lord. So they took everything from the hand of Ezra and went with it to Jerusalem.

8.7.1.en: He asked the men to hand over all they had by weight with all exactness, not out of doubt of their faithfulness, but so that no one would doubt them and everything would reach the house of the Lord accurately.

8.7.3.en: 31- Then we departed from the river of Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, to go unto Jerusalem: and the hand of our God was upon us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy, and of such as lay in wait by the way. 32- And we came to Jerusalem, and abode there three days. 33- Now on the fourth day was the silver and the gold and the vessels weighed in the house of our God by the hand of Meremoth the son of Uriah the priest; and with him was Eleazar the son of Phinehas; and with them was Jozabad the son of Jeshua, and Noadiah the son of Binnui, Levites;

8.7.4.en: 34- By number and by weight of every one: and all the weight was written at that time. 35- Also the children of those that had been carried away, which were come out of the captivity, offered burnt offerings unto the God of Israel, twelve bullocks for all Israel, ninety and six rams, seventy and seven lambs, twelve he goats for a sin offering: all this was a burnt offering unto the LORD. 36- And they delivered the king's commissions unto the king's lieutenants, and to the governors on this side the river: and they furthered the people, and the house of God.

8.8.0.en: After the Jews gathered with Ezra at the river Ahava and fasted, prayed and humbled themselves, the journey set out on the twelfth of the first month, which is the month of Nisan, corresponding to the month of April in the Gregorian year, and arrived at Jerusalem on the first of the fifth month, which is the month of Ab, corresponding to the month of August (ch. 7:9); that is, the journey took about four months.

8.8.1.en: Ezra did not give us details about the journey to Jerusalem, because this journey signifies our journey in the world until we reach the heavenly Jerusalem. And when we arrive, the period of our life on earth becomes as nothing before the glory of heaven; so also the journey of Ezra, whatever its troubles, is worth nothing compared with their enjoyment of seeing the holy city and the temple of God.

8.8.2.en: All that Ezra mentions about the journey is that God preserved them from all dangers, whether the enemies, that is, the nations that did not love the Jews, or those who lay in wait by the way, that is, robbers, for the hand of God was caring for them as long as they sought the worship of God and to please Him.

8.8.3.en: The journey of Ezra from Babylon to Jerusalem resembles the journey of Moses from Egypt to the land of Canaan, but the journey of Moses took forty years, while the journey of Ezra was four months. Moses had with him the ark of the covenant of God, the pillar of cloud, the pillar of fire, the rock of water and the manna, but Ezra, who is a second Moses, had with him the hand of God, who preserved them as He preserved the first Moses and his people.

8.8.4.en: Ezra enjoyed the hand of God that preserved him and his people because he spent three days in prayer, fasting and repentance, and his goal was clear, which was to reach Jerusalem, for God preserves His children and those who seek Him and hold fast to Him.

8.9.0.en: After the journey reached Jerusalem, they spent three days there; they did not go to their towns where their fathers had lived in Judea. What did they do in the three days?

8.9.1.en: 1- They thanked God, who had preserved them throughout the journey from all dangers.

8.9.2.en: 2- Perhaps they contemplated the temple which they had long yearned to see and had heard about from their fathers and forefathers.

8.9.3.en: And of course it is understood that the Jews who had preceded them and settled in Jerusalem welcomed them and hosted them during these three days.

8.9.4.en: Those returning enjoyed unity, because they began the journey with prayer, fasting and repentance, so they felt their unity within the hand of God on their journey.

8.10.0.en: After thanking God for three days, Ezra handed over, through the twelve men whom he had entrusted with the silver, the gold and the vessels, and gave them to the priests and Levites, the servants of the temple and those in charge of the treasury.

8.10.1.en: We notice the exactness in the handing over of these treasures, for he handed them over by number and by weight, so that his faithfulness and the faithfulness of the men with him would not be doubted, and they wrote down the particulars of what they handed over, to be kept inside the temple for whoever should come after him or deal with these possessions.

8.11.0.en: After that they offered sacrifices of thanksgiving to God, who had preserved them on the way and let them enjoy seeing His holy temple.

8.11.1.en: They offered twelve bullocks for all Israel, and although those returning were from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, the Jews after the return from captivity had become one state, even if those returning from the other tribes were very few, because affliction creates unity and love among those who were divided.

8.11.2.en: They offered burnt offerings to God to declare their inclination to consecrate their hearts to God. And they offered sin offerings, as a declaration of their repentance and their need of God's forgiveness, so their feelings were love and humility.

8.12.0.en: The satraps: the civil chiefs among the Persians.

8.12.1.en: Ezra delivered the orders of King Artaxerxes to the satraps and governors beyond the river, who were responsible for the region where the Jews lived, and they carried out the royal orders at once and supported the Jews with the financial needs from the royal treasuries, and also their needs of foodstuffs. Thus by the grace of God hearts that were hostile to the Jews were changed into hearts that help and support the Jews.

8.12.2.en: If you live by faith and rely on God, He is able to turn whoever is hostile to you, or does you wrong, into a person who cooperates with you and helps you, so that you may be reassured and grow in your love for God and thank Him at all times.

9.0.0.en: When Ezra heard of the spread of foreign marriages among his people, he was deeply affected, and sorrow filled his heart, so he did the following:

9.0.1.en: 1- I rent my garment and my mantle: that is, he tore all his clothes, and this is an old custom in the countries of the East and still continues to this day in some parts of Upper Egypt, as an expression of his not enduring the distress and having no appearance to boast of, but expressing his torn heart by torn outer garments.

9.0.2.en: The Bible tells us of many who tore their clothes in difficult situations, such as Reuben, when he did not find his brother Joseph in the pit (Gen 37:29), and Jacob when he saw Joseph's coat stained with blood (Gen 37:43), and also Jephthah the Gileadite, who vowed to offer as a sacrifice the first who met him after his victory in the war, and found his daughter (Judg 11:35), and also Job when calamities covered him (Job 1:20).

9.0.3.en: 2- And plucked off the hair of my head and of my beard:

9.0.4.en: Another old custom of the East as an expression of intense grief, for the beard represents dignity and the hair of the head represents a crown, especially among women, as happened with Job when afflictions came upon him (Job 1:20).

9.0.6.en: Because he had the authority to punish the traitors and command them to leave their foreign wives, but at the same time he saw the weakness of his people and that they might not endure this punishment, so they would leave God because of their attachment to their wives and children and join the Gentiles and worship idols. Therefore he expressed his grief within himself and punished no one, but after thirteen years the spiritual condition of the people improved, so Nehemiah was able to command those married to foreign women to separate from their wives, and he even punished them harshly and struck them and plucked off their hair, and they obeyed him.

9.0.7.en: Ezra's astonishment was increased by how the people had not learned from their fathers who married foreign women, so God allowed them the captivity to discipline them.

9.0.8.en: He was also astonished at how the people could violate the Law while they lived around the holy temple of God, that is, how they did not fear God.

9.0.9.en: And finally he was astonished because he knows the longsuffering of God but also knows His justice and that His anger is severe, so how would this people endure the punishment of God if they did not repent?

9.0.10.en: Ezra remained astonished, not knowing whether to rebuke them, how to rebuke them, and how not to lose them, having compassion on their weakness, for he wanted their salvation by any means.

9.0.11.en: Here Ezra's fatherhood and his feeling as a servant for his people appear, for he was not content with not sinning himself, but with love humbled himself before God, that God might have mercy on His people, that is, His children.

9.1.0.en: The people heard of Ezra's humbling of himself because of his knowledge of the presence of pagan marriages among them, and the following happened:

9.1.1.en: 1- One group whose heart was moved and who feared God behaved like Ezra, for they gathered around him praying and humbling themselves before God that He might have mercy on His people and forgive the offenders.

9.1.2.en: 2- Another group of the people was not affected by Ezra's humbling of himself.

9.1.3.en: 3- A third group remained immersed in sin, indulging evil lusts and pagan marriages.

9.1.4.en: Those who feared God gathered around Ezra and found him humbled and astonished, as we mentioned in the previous verse, and the Bible's repetition of "his sitting astonished" confirms that he continued for a long time in prayer, humbling himself and astonishment.

9.1.5.en: Ezra continued in his humbling of himself until the evening and was probably fasting, that is, he spent his whole day in fasting, prayer, repentance and supplication before God for his people.

9.2.0.en: When the time of the evening offering came, Ezra felt hope, so he arose, lifting his heart to God in the form of this burnt offering which is offered in the evening to please God; that is, he arose to propitiate God by his humbling of himself, namely his torn garments and his submission in his prostration and in his prayer, with his hands spread out before God. He felt that he had no refuge but God, so he poured out his prayers, his tears and his astonishment and committed himself to God, asking for His intervention to cleanse his people and deliver them from their sins.

9.2.1.en: Ezra's prostration and spreading out of his hands in prayer signifies Christ in the Garden of Gethsemane, when He prostrated Himself and prayed with many tears for the sins of His people. Ezra also resembles Moses, who spread out his hands and prayed until his people prevailed over Amalek.

9.2.2.en: God looks at your closet, waiting for you to prostrate yourself before Him and offer repentance for your sins and supplications for all whom you love, and He answers the tears that are poured out and the soul that is broken before Him.

9.3.0.en: Ezra, in his fatherhood to the people, felt that he was responsible for their sins, because as a spiritual leader he is responsible to teach his people and warn them of sins. So he offers repentance for his own shortcoming and not only intercession for his sinning people, and he declared his shame and confusion before God because of these sins. This is a prayer of repentance and confession before God, and it carries two meanings:

9.3.1.en: 1- Ezra's confession of the sins of his people, offering repentance on their behalf.

9.3.3.en: 3- His sense of the holiness of God, before which he is ashamed to stand.

9.3.4.en: 4- His humility, in his looking to the ground and his inability to lift his face toward God.

9.3.5.en: Ezra also declares, as one of the people, that their sins have risen over their heads, and have grown up to the heavens. This means the following:

9.3.6.en: 1- The spread of sin among the people, even if a number of them had fallen into pagan marriage, there may be others who had fallen by sight, or thought, or any degree of adultery.

9.3.7.en: 2- Sin humbles man, rises over his head and defiles him.

9.3.8.en: 3- Sin provokes God by growing up to the heavens.

9.3.9.en: 4- Sin spread among the people and many fell into it, so it grew up to the heavens. In this they resemble the people of Sodom and Gomorrah, whose sins rose up to heaven, so they deserved to die by burning (Gen 18:20). This means Ezra's declaration of his confession of the sin because of which they deserve destruction, but he asks for the mercies of God and His forgiveness.

9.3.10.en: Ezra asks nothing of God, but confesses his sins as a son in shame before the greatness of his Father, who loves him.

9.3.11.en: Ezra here is a type of Christ, the righteous and holy, who bore the sins of His people, although He had not sinned in anything.

9.4.0.en: Our kings and our priests: our civil and spiritual leaders.

9.4.1.en: The kings of the lands: the kings of the empires that enslaved the Jews, such as Assyria and Babylon. Ezra continues his confession and declares two things:

9.4.2.en: 1- The deep rootedness of the sin of association with pagan practices since the days of the fathers.

9.4.3.en: 2- This sin is abominable and deserved a severe punishment, which was captivity and destruction when the fathers committed this sin. Consequently the sin that took place in the days of Ezra deserves the same punishment, which is destruction, bondage and plunder. It is a confession by Ezra that God is merciful and did not punish them according to their sins despite their doing this abominable sin.

9.5.0.en: From the LORD: the presence of God.

9.5.1.en: A nail (peg): a piece of wood by which the tent is fixed in the ground.

9.5.2.en: The sins of the people of God had been abominable for many years, and God was very longsuffering toward them, but He allowed them to be disciplined, and His wrath came upon them, but for a very short time which God likens to a moment, until they repented and returned to Him. The period of captivity is very short and counts for nothing before the mercies of God, which He gives to His people forever in His Kingdom.

9.5.3.en: And if sin drove the people out of the land that God had given them, God returns and brings them back to it and establishes them in it, as the tent is fixed by the peg in the ground, on condition that they remain holding fast to His commandments, as He establishes those who believe in Him in His Church forever, as long as they hold fast to Him. The moment is the discipline of the captivity, and the peg is the commandments of God and His Law in the Old Testament, to which are added in the New Testament the Holy Sacraments.

9.5.4.en: The aim of God's discipline and mercy is that we may take heed and reject sin, so that we become spiritually enlightened, see God and enjoy fellowship with Him, and spend our few days on earth, which are a preparation for heaven, where we enter into glories forever, before which all the toils of the little earth become light.

9.5.5.en: Turning away from God and falling into sin, which led to the captivity, is a time of darkness, while returning to Jerusalem and worshiping God in His temple is enlightenment, and it is the life that the people receive in the times of their worship of God in the midst of the bondage to which they are subject in Assyria, Babylon, then Media and Persia.

9.6.0.en: The mercy of God is revealed in His people through His care for them, although they were enslaved to the kings of Assyria, Babylon and Persia, so God intervenes miraculously and moves the kings of Persia, namely Cyrus and Darius, then Artaxerxes, to bring the people of God back to Jerusalem, encourage them and give them the vessels of the house of the Lord and money and timber and many gifts, that they might build the temple and worship God.

9.6.1.en: The people did not only return to Jerusalem, but built the temple in the days of Zerubbabel, then by worship in the days of Ezra, and finally God gave them a wall in Jerusalem, meaning God's protection of them, which also appeared when Nehemiah built the wall of Jerusalem and its gates.

9.7.0.en: Seek not their peace: do not make treaties of peace or alliances with them.

9.7.1.en: Ezra continues his confession on behalf of all the people, saying: What shall we say before Your many mercies, which brought us back from captivity and built the temple for us and care for us and give us all our needs? But, to our shame, before this wonderful love we disobeyed You and abandoned Your commandments, because You declared to us that the land of Canaan, which You would cause us to possess, is an unclean land through the worship of idols by those who dwell in it and all the sins connected with it, and that these sins are spread everywhere in this land.

9.7.2.en: And You commanded us not to be joined in pagan marriages, as Your prophets declared to us, such as Moses the prophet (Deut 7:1-3), and not to be joined with the pagan inhabitants of the land in treaties and alliances, indeed not to mingle with them, that we might live in our faith in the one God and in our upright conduct, and not imitate the sins of the pagans. And You promised to support us and protect us, so that we would be strong and receive the good things of the land, and even leave it as an inheritance to our children, as long as we were obedient to Your commandments.

9.8.0.en: Ezra also confesses that the divine discipline by captivity is less than what the sins of his people deserve, so he declares his confession of the abominableness of the sins that led God to punish the people with captivity. But even after He punished, His mercies appeared in bringing back the remnant of them, that is, those who love God and worship in His house, through the return to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel, then Ezra.

9.9.0.en: Ezra denounces what his people did by returning to the breaking of God's commandments and intermarrying with pagan women. And he declares that they deserve a greater punishment, that even the remnant that returned to Jerusalem should perish, because it was defiled by the worship of idols; for rejecting God's commandments is a rejection of His person and a declaration of the people's lack of love for Him, for whoever accepts the commandment accepts God who gave it.

9.10.0.en: At the close of the prayer Ezra confesses the righteousness of God and His tenderness, which appeared in His leaving a remnant for His people, that is, those returning from captivity, whom He helped and for whom He built the temple, that they might worship Him in it.

9.10.1.en: Ezra affirmed that their sin was upon their heads, in shame and confusion before God, and he committed his life and the people to God, because they deserved every punishment because of marriage to foreign women, and he did not ask for mercy from God or help because of his sense of the shame of sin; and in confidence he left his life and his people in the hands of God, believing in His fatherhood, which would not forsake or neglect them. He felt it a great honor that God allowed him to stand and pray before Him, so he could not ask for more than this. It is a wonderful humility and an example of broken prayer and true repentance before God.

9.10.2.en: To the extent of your humility, your confession of your sins and your humbling of yourself before God, you receive many mercies, so do not let your day end before you examine yourself and confess before God, and you will receive His forgiveness and blessings.

9.10.4.en: 1- The book began in the first chapter by telling us of the first return to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel, then the building of the temple.

9.10.5.en: 2- It tells us in the seventh chapter of the return to Jerusalem under Ezra.

9.10.6.en: 3- This chapter tells us of Ezra the shepherd, broken in prayer and firm in the care of his people, to cleanse them of evil by putting away the pagan marriages and all the sins connected with them, so he was able to draw the hearts of the people to himself and they obeyed him, and so they received the mercies of God.
